html:
Grouped by depth. The answers are the short version you would actually say out loud; each points at the module with the detail.

Fundamentals

What are the three ownership rules?

Every value has exactly one owner; there is only one owner at a time; when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped. Together they give memory safety without a garbage collector.

What is the difference between &T and &mut T?

&T is a shared, read-only borrow — many may exist at once. &mut T is an exclusive borrow — exactly one, and no shared borrows may coexist. The exclusivity is what makes data races impossible to express.

Why can't you have &mut and & at the same time?

Because the compiler's guarantee to a &mut holder is "nobody else can observe this value". Without it, &mut could not be optimised or safely sent across threads.

What does the borrow checker actually check?

That every reference is valid for its whole use (no dangling), and that aliasing-plus-mutation never happens simultaneously. It does this with lifetimes, which are regions of code, not runtime values.

When do you need explicit lifetimes?

When the compiler cannot infer which input a returned reference derives from — typically a function with two or more reference inputs returning a reference, or a struct storing a reference.

String vs &str?

String owns a heap buffer and is growable. &str is a borrowed view (pointer + length) into UTF-8 owned by someone else. Take &str in parameters; return String when you must allocate.

Why can't you index a String with s[0]?

Because a String is UTF-8 and there is no single obvious meaning for "element 0" — byte 0, code point 0, or grapheme 0 all differ. Use chars(), bytes(), or s.get(0..n) which returns Option.

Option<T> vs null?

Option is an enum in the type system: the compiler forces you to handle None. There is no implicit null, no NullPointerException, and Option<&T> costs nothing extra thanks to niche optimisation.

Type system

impl Trait vs dyn Trait?

impl Trait is static dispatch — monomorphised per type, inlined, zero cost, but cannot hold heterogeneous values. dyn Trait is a fat pointer with a vtable — one indirect call, one copy of the code, works in a Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>.

What is monomorphisation, and its downside?

Generics are compiled once per concrete type, which is why they are fast. The costs are binary size and compile time.

What makes a trait object-safe?

No generic methods, no methods returning Self, no associated constants. Anything that would require knowing the concrete type at the call site breaks the vtable.

Associated type vs generic parameter?

An associated type allows exactly one implementation per type (Iterator::Item). A generic parameter allows several (Add<i32> and Add<f64>).

What does Sized mean, and why ?Sized?

Sized means the size is known at compile time. str, [T] and dyn Trait are unsized, so a generic taking them by value needs ?Sized and a reference.

Why can't you implement a foreign trait for a foreign type?

The orphan rule: at least one of the trait or the type must be local to your crate. It prevents two crates from providing conflicting impls.

Memory and pointers

Box vs Rc vs Arc?

Box is unique ownership with one heap allocation. Rc is reference-counted sharing on one thread (non-atomic counter). Arc is the atomic version, safe across threads, ~10–20× more expensive to clone.

When do you need RefCell?

When you must mutate through a shared reference and cannot express it with the compile-time borrow checker — e.g. a graph or an observer list. Borrows are checked at runtime and panic on violation.

What is interior mutability, and its cost?

Mutating through &T using Cell/RefCell/Mutex/atomics. Cell is free; RefCell costs a runtime flag check; Mutex costs a lock.

How do you leak memory in safe Rust?

Create an Rc cycle. Two Rcs pointing at each other never reach zero. Break it with Weak.

What is Drop, and when does it run?

A destructor trait, run when the owner goes out of scope, in reverse declaration order, including during unwinding from a panic. It is why RAII works for locks, files and transactions.

Concurrency

Send vs Sync?

Send: the value can be moved to another thread. Sync: &T can be shared between threads. Rc is neither; Arc<T> is both when T: Send + Sync.

How does Rust prevent data races?

A data race needs two threads, one writing, no synchronisation. That requires &mut accessible from two threads, or a shared borrow alongside a mutation — both forbidden. Send/Sync extend the argument across thread boundaries.

Mutex<T> vs RwLock<T>?

Mutex allows one accessor of any kind; RwLock allows many readers or one writer. RwLock only wins when reads dominate and critical sections are long enough for contention to matter.

What is mutex poisoning?

If a thread panics while holding the lock, the mutex is marked poisoned and later lock() calls return Err. into_inner() on the error recovers the data.

Threads vs async — when each?

Threads for CPU-bound work and a small number of long-running tasks; async for many concurrent I/O waits. Async multiplexes waiting; it does not speed up computation.

What does async fn return, and when does it run?

A Future — a state machine. Nothing runs until something polls it (.await or a runtime).

Why must futures be Pinned?

A future's states may contain references into itself. Moving it after polling would invalidate those references, so Pin guarantees a stable address.

What happens when you select! and one branch loses?

The losing future is dropped, which is cancellation. If it was mid-operation, you can get a partial write — which is why non-cancellable work should be spawned.

Errors and API design

panic! vs Result?

panic! is for programmer errors and violated invariants. Result is for expected failures the caller can act on. "File not found" is a Result; "index out of bounds in code that checked the length" is a panic.

thiserror vs anyhow?

thiserror derives a typed error enum for libraries — callers can match on variants. anyhow is a boxed dynamic error with context for applications. Never expose anyhow in a public library API.

Why #[non_exhaustive] on a public error enum?

So you can add variants without a breaking change, since downstream matches are not exhaustive.

Why should a handler return a generic message on 5xx?

To avoid leaking internals (SQL text, file paths, stack frames) to a client. Log the real error server-side.

What is a smart constructor?

A fn parse(...) -> Result<Email, Error> that validates and returns a newtype. It makes invalid states unrepresentable: any Email in the type system is valid.

Performance

Why are iterators as fast as loops?

After inlining, the iterator chain becomes the same machine code, minus the bounds checks that the compiler can now prove unnecessary.

What are zero-cost abstractions here, and which are not?

Free: iterators, generics, newtypes, Option<&T>. Not free: dyn dispatch, Box/Rc/Arc, format!, RefCell, clone().

How would you find a performance problem?

Profile first: perf or cargo flamegraph, or samply for async. Find the widest leaf frame. Only then change code, and re-measure with criterion.

When is clone() the wrong answer?

When it hides a design problem — usually a function that should borrow instead of own, or a struct that should hold an Arc.

What is the biggest single performance win available?

Choosing the right algorithm and data structure. HashSet instead of a linear scan is 1000×; no compiler flag competes.

Ecosystem and practice

How do you structure a large Rust project?

A workspace with a domain crate that has no I/O (fast tests, stable API), plus api and worker binaries. Logic in lib.rs, main.rs thin.

What does cargo clippy -D warnings in CI buy you?

A consistent floor of idiom and a class of bugs caught before review — redundant_clone, ptr_arg, large_enum_variant, unwrap_used.

How do you test an HTTP handler without a network?

app.oneshot(request) with tower::ServiceExt. It runs routing, extractors, middleware and error mapping in-process.

How do you handle schema changes safely?

Migrations that are additive and reversible: add nullable columns, backfill, then constrain. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY for large tables. Never edit an applied migration — checksums will reject it.

Why commit Cargo.lock for a binary?

Reproducible builds. cargo build --locked in CI then fails if a dependency would change, which is exactly the alert you want.

Questions to ask them

A good signal in an interview is asking about the hard parts:

  • What is your compile time, and what have you done about it?
  • Where does async hurt you most?
  • How do you handle the Send + 'static boundary in spawned tasks?
  • Do you use unsafe anywhere, and how is it reviewed?
  • What is your policy on adding dependencies?
